name: Western University
candidates: The initial aspirations of Bishop Hellmuth carry through to the internationally known research of our top scholars today. These leaders of vision, courage and imagination have always looked to the future in shaping Western University. Founded on March 7, 1878 by Bishop Isaac Hellmuth (1817–1901) ‘The Western University of London Ontario’ opened its doors to students for the first time in 1881. Four faculties – Arts, Divinity, Law and Medicine were there at Western's inception. In 1916, the current campus was purchased from the Kingsmill family, and in 1923 the university was renamed The University of Western Ontario. Since that first class graduated in 1883, the university has become a vibrant centre of learning. Through 12 faculties and three affiliated university colleges, Western today offers its 36,000-plus students more than 400 specializations, majors and minors. It was at Western where Sir Frederick Banting rose from a restless sleep in 1920 and wrote out 25 words that led to his discovery of insulin. It was at Western where researchers led by Ivan Smith developed the world’s first ‘cobalt bomb’ to treat cancer in 1951. This discovery increased the cure rate for cervical cancer to 75 per cent from 25 per cent. And while our excellence roots itself in history, Western continues to eye the next-generation discoveries. Western, a leader in wind engineering since 1965, testing such structures as the World Trade Center, Sears Tower and Jakarta Tower. Western Engineering will continue its dominance with the opening of the WindEEE Dome research facility. Western leads at home and abroad thanks to construction of a state-of-the-art Richard Ivey School of Business in 2012. North America’s first business school campus opened in Hong Kong in 1998. Western has continued to push innovation. In 2012 a HIV vaccine developed by Dr. Chil-Yong Kang received approval by the United States Food and Drug Administration to start human clinical trials. Western has been a medical advancement leader since 1878.

name: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST)
candidates: Abstract Understanding how neural networks rely on visual cues offers a human-interpretable view of their internal decision processes. The cue-conflict benchmark has been influential in probing shape-texture preference and in motivating the insight that stronger, human-like shape bias is often associated with improved in-domain performance. However, we find that the current stylization-based instantiation can yield unstable and ambiguous bias estimates. Specifically, stylization may not reliably instantiate perceptually valid and separable cues nor control their relative informativeness, ratio-based bias can obscure absolute cue sensitivity, and restricting evaluation to preselected classes can distort model predictions by ignoring the full decision space. Together, these factors can confound preference with cue validity, cue balance, and recognizability artifacts. We introduce REFINED-BIAS, an integrated dataset and evaluation framework for reliable and interpretable shape-texture bias diagnosis. REFINED-BIAS constructs balanced, human- and model-recognizable cue pairs using explicit definitions of shape and texture, and measures cue-specific sensitivity over the full label space via a ranking-based metric, enabling fairer cross-model comparisons. Across diverse training regimes and architectures, REFINED-BIAS enables fairer cross-model comparison, more faithful diagnosis of shape and texture biases, and clearer empirical conclusions, resolving inconsistencies that prior cue-conflict evaluations could not reliably disambiguate. A widely used benchmark for evaluating how AI recognizes objects may give researchers a misleading picture of how their models interpret visual information. A new study identifies flaws in the test that help explain conflicting findings about AI's reliance on shape and texture. Led by Professor Jaejun Yoo of the Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence at UNIST, the team introduced REFINED-BIAS, a new benchmark that measures how effectively AI models recognize shape and texture separately, rather than relying on relative preference alone. The study revisits cue-conflict testing, introduced in 2019 to examine whether AI models recognize objects by their shape or surface texture. Using images such as a cat's outline covered in elephant skin, early studies suggested that models favoring shape tended to perform better at image recognition. Subsequent research, however, produced conflicting results. The researchers found that the benchmark's scoring method can obscure important differences between models. One that correctly identifies shape eight times and texture twice receives the same 80% shape-bias score as another that identifies shape 80 times and texture 20 times, despite their markedly different recognition abilities. The test images can also distort results when shape and texture are poorly separated or one cue is easier to recognize. Its scoring method further restricts predictions to selected categories, potentially misrepresenting a model's actual response. To address these shortcomings, the team assembled **6,000 images across 20 object categories**, carefully separating shape and texture cues while keeping them recognizable to humans and AI models. REFINED-BIAS also uses a ranking-based metric to measure sensitivity to each cue across the model's full range of predictions. The results revealed that models with higher recognition accuracy generally showed greater sensitivity to both shape and texture. The framework also more consistently captured the effects of shape-focused training and revealed stronger shape recognition in certain newer vision architectures and large-scale pretrained models. “Benchmarks do more than measure AI performance. They also shape how researchers develop and improve models,” said Professor Yoo. “We hope REFINED-BIAS will provide a more reliable picture of how AI uses shape and texture, helping guide future work on model architecture and training.” The study, with Pum Jun Kim and Seung-Ah Lee of AIGS as co-first authors, was selected for a Spotlight presentation at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2026), a distinction awarded to approximately 1.3% of the 10,473 submissions. The work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP), the Artificial Intelligence Graduate School Program (UNIST), and the InnoCORE program, with funding from the Ministry of Science and ICT. Journal Reference Pum Jun Kim, Seung-Ah Lee, Seongho Park, et al. , “On the Reliability of Cue Conflict and Beyond,” ECCV’26 (2026).

Abstract Flexible and foldable displays require optically clear adhesives (OCAs) that combine ultrahigh optical transparency with mechanical resilience under repeated deformation. However, conventional acrylic-based OCAs often fail to achieve both properties simultaneously. Herein, we synthesized a polyurethane diacrylate (PUDA) crosslinker incorporating biomass-derived isosorbide and photostable 1,3-bis(isocyanatomethyl)cyclohexane (H6XDI) for flexible display adhesives. The segmented polyurethane architecture forms a mechanically flexible yet robust network, enabling rapid strain recovery while maintaining ultrahigh optical transparency. Furthermore, the incorporation of an isosorbide-based PUDA crosslinker introduces a biomass-derived component and preserves excellent optical properties due to its intrinsically low birefringence. As a result, the PUDA crosslinked OCA exhibits exceptional optical transmittance (99.8%) and maintains high transparency (98.6%) even at 50% tensile strain, alongside low modulus, stable adhesion, and clean debonding behavior. These results highlight the potential of PUDA OCAs for high-performance and energy-efficient foldable display applications. An adhesive developed at UNIST remains nearly transparent even when stretched to 50% beyond its original length and recovers its shape within 2.5 seconds after repeated stretching. Designed for foldable and rollable displays, the material combines exceptional optical clarity with the flexibility needed to withstand repeated deformation. Led by Professor Dong Woog Lee of the School of Energy and Chemical Engineering at UNIST, the research team developed the optically clear adhesive (OCA) using a polyurethane diacrylate (PUDA) crosslinker containing isosorbide, a compound derived from biomass such as corn and wheat starch. Optically clear adhesives hold together the layers of a display, including protective glass, touch sensors, and panels. They must remain transparent while accommodating repeated bending and stretching, a combination that conventional acrylic-based adhesives often struggle to achieve. The new material transmits 99.8% of light, retaining 98.6% transmittance even when stretched by 50%. Under the same strain, an adhesive containing a conventional HDDA crosslinker transmitted just 71.9%. After 100 cycles of stretching to 20% beyond its original length, the adhesive returned to its initial dimensions within 2.5 seconds. The HDDA-based adhesive took more than 100 seconds to recover under comparable conditions. The difference lies in the crosslinker's molecular structure. Isosorbide has low birefringence, helping the adhesive remain optically clear as it stretches. The flexible polyurethane segments also keep polymer chains farther apart, reducing interactions that would otherwise slow their recovery. The adhesive showed bonding strength comparable to commercial products. When tested in a flexible display module, it endured 10,000 folding cycles without visible cracks, wrinkles, or separation between layers. It could also be removed cleanly after heat treatment at 80 °C, leaving no visible residue and potentially making display components easier to recover or reuse. “Display adhesives must transmit light efficiently while withstanding repeated deformation,” said Professor Lee. “Our material could help enable brighter, more energy-efficient foldable and rollable displays with improved durability.” Yoonji Choi of the School of Energy and Chemical Engineering at UNIST served as the first author of the study, while Dr. Myung-Jin Bae as a co-corresponding author. Supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) and the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), the findings were published online in Advanced Science on August 30, 2026. Journal Reference Yoonji Choi, Geonwoo Lee, Yeonseo Kim, et al ., “Isosorbide-Based Optically Clear Adhesives With Ultrahigh Transparency and Rapid Strain Recovery for Flexible Displays,” Adv. Sci., (2026).

Abstract Thermal operations are quantum channels that play a central role in deriving thermodynamic limitations in quantum systems. However, they were originally defined by implementation procedures rather than by fundamental principles. Alternative models of thermal processes have been proposed, but they obscure the resources required for implementation. Here, we identify the universal principle that separates these models. We show that thermal operations are uniquely characterized by a purely quantum information-theoretic property, which we call informational equilibrium. This formulation does not assume a particular Hamiltonian or even a notion of temperature: a channel is a thermal operation precisely when it leaves its environment invariant whenever the system is prepared in equilibrium. In this way, the usual energetic description of equilibrium (i.e., Gibbs states) emerges as a representation of an underlying informational constraint. Extending this framework, we note that enforcing environment invariance for all system inputs leads to catalytic channels, which idealize perfectly reusable heat baths. This informational equilibrium perspective culminates in a hierarchy for doubly-stochastic quantum channels, with strict separations between the classes. Our refined hierarchy sharpens the failure of the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem in the quantum regime, and highlights the richer structural landscape of quantum channels compared to classical stochastic processes that cannot be captured by state-convertibility relations. A quantum process can preserve thermal equilibrium without necessarily being achievable through interactions with a heat bath alone. Professor Seok Hyung Lie of the Department of Physics at UNIST, working with colleagues in Singapore and Germany, has identified a fundamental principle that explains this distiction. The study introduces informational equilibrium, a condition that characterizes thermal operations without requiring temperature or energy levels to be specified in advance. Thermal operations describe processes in which a quantum system exchanges energy with an environment in thermal equilibrium while conserving their combined energy. They belong to a broader class known as Gibbs-preserving maps, which leave a system unchanged when it is already in thermal equilibrium. Yet not every Gibbs-preserving map can be implemented as a thermal operation. The researchers found that the distinction depends on whether the environment can remain unchanged. They proved that a quantum process is a thermal operation precisely when it can be implemented without altering the environment whenever the system starts in equilibrium. This condition, termed informational equilibrium, provides a mathematical characterization of thermal operations independent of their conventional energy-based definition. For Gibbs-preserving maps that fall outside this class, preserving the system's equilibrium state necessarily comes at a cost: the environment must change. Such processes therefore require resources beyond those available through thermal operations alone. The framework also clarifies the limits of **quantum catalysis**, in which an auxiliary quantum system enables a transformation while returning to its original state. The researchers showed that a catalyst cannot extend the range of thermal operations if it must be restored exactly even when the system's initial state contains small errors. Any catalytic advantage beyond those limits must therefore depend on sensitivity to those errors. “Our study shows that thermal operations can be understood through an informational condition, without specifying temperature or the energy levels of individual quantum states,” said Professor Lie. “This distinction could help establish the resources needed to operate quantum devices and assess the performance limits of quantum heat engines.” Published in Physical Review Letters on July 13, the study also involved Professor Nelly H. Y. Ng of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, researcher Jeongrak Son of Freie Universität Berlin, Professor Henrik Wilming of Leibniz University Hannover, and independent researcher Paul Boes. The research was supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP), and the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF). Journal Reference Seok Hyung Lie, Jeongrak Son, Paul Boes, et al., "Thermal Operations from Informational Equilibrium," Phys. Rev. Lett., (2026).

Abstract Hybrid tin oxo clusters (SnOCs) have emerged as promising molecular resists for electron-beam (EB) and extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography; However, their patterning mechanisms remain poorly understood due to the coupled effects of ligand electronics, cluster nuclearity, and electron-induced fragmentation. In this study, we demonstrate a ligand-mediated nuclearity tuning strategy that enables the selective synthesis of Sn6- and Sn3-based clusters using electron-donating carboxylate and electron-withdrawing diphenylphosphinate ligands, respectively. Density functional theory calculations, electrostatic potential analysis, and bond dissociation energy evaluations show that ligand electronic properties dictate the preferred electron-driven cleavage pathways. Sn6 clusters predominantly undergo Sn–alkyl bond scission, whereas aromatic phosphinate ligands in Sn3 clusters stabilize the framework and suppress ligand fragmentation. These trends are supported by As a result, Sn6 clusters exhibit high EB sensitivity (D0 = 285 µC cm−2) and sub-30 nm resolution, while Sn3 clusters deliver ultra-low line-edge roughness (1.02 nm) and excellent pattern fidelity. This work identifies nuclearity as a chemically tunable parameter for rational molecular-resist design. The organic molecules surrounding tin atoms can determine how a photoresist responds to electron exposure—and how precisely it reproduces a semiconductor pattern. A research team, led by Professor Ji-Hyun Jang of the School of Energy and Chemical Engineering at UNIST found that changing these molecules alters the structure and patterning behavior of tin-based resists being explored for next-generation extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Tin-based photoresists have attracted interest for EUV lithography because they absorb EUV radiation efficiently and can withstand the etching processes used to transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers. Yet the chemical reactions that govern their sensitivity and pattern quality have remained difficult to understand. To investigate these reactions, the researchers compared two ligands with contrasting electronic properties. An electron-donating ligand derived from adamantane-1-carboxylic acid produced clusters containing six tin atoms (Sn6), while an electron-withdrawing diphenylphosphinate ligand produced clusters containing three (Sn3). The difference in molecular structure translated into distinct patterning behavior. The Sn6-based resist responded at a lower electron-beam dose, producing patterns with a designed line width of 20 nanometers. The Sn3-based resist required a higher dose but produced smoother edges, with a line-edge roughness of just 1.02 nanometers in 50-nanometer-wide lines. The team then examined how the clusters reacted to electron exposure. In Sn6, tin–alkyl bonds broke readily, promoting crosslinking between organic and inorganic components. This reaction helped explain the material's higher sensitivity. Sn3 behaved differently. Its aromatic phosphinate ligands resisted fragmentation and helped preserve the tin–oxygen–phosphorus framework, limiting the chemical changes that can disrupt pattern formation. This stability contributed to greater pattern fidelity and smoother edges. Computational analysis and chemical measurements supported these findings, linking the ligands' electronic properties to the different reactions observed in the two materials. “Our findings show that photoresist sensitivity and pattern precision depend on ligand chemistry as well as tin content,” said Professor Jang. “This could help guide the design of EUV photoresists for different manufacturing requirements.” Published online in Small on August 25, the study was also selected for the journal's back cover. It was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP), the 2026 Research Fund of UNIST, and the InnoCORE program of the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT). Journal Reference Seong-Ji Ha, Jin Young Lee, Bo Kyu Kwon, et al., "Ligand-Mediated Nuclearity Tuning of Tin Oxo Clusters for Advanced Lithography," (2026).

name: Sunway University
candidates: The origins of Sunway Education can be traced back to 1987 with the establishment of Sunway College in Petaling Jaya, Malaysia by Tan Sri Dr Sir Jeffrey Cheah KBE AO. Since then, Sunway Education has grown to be a leading provider of quality education and research in Malaysia and the region with aspirations to be a global contributor to high-end sustainable solutions and good planetary health.

In 2016, the Jeffrey Cheah Foundation entered into a partnership with the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network Association (SDSN) and Professor Jeffrey Sachs, renowned economist and Director of the SDSN. With the partnership, the Jeffrey Sachs Center on Sustainable Development was established at Sunway University to create and deliver the world’s best academic and executive programs on sustainable development. In 2019, Sunway University became the centre to the UN SDSN for the Asia region, alongside centres in Paris representing Europe and New York for the Americas.

To further enhance our commitment to the sustainability agenda and preserving our planet for our future generations, Sunway Education Group in 2021 established the Sunway Centre for Planetary Health which focuses on bringing interdisciplinary approaches to bear on mitigating future risks posed by pandemics and other worldwide health challenges.

name: The Education University of Hong Kong
HSE University
candidates: The first attempt involved creating a department of economic theory at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (1989-90) and the MSU faculties of physics and history (1990-91). Students took courses taught by young lecturers who were recent graduates of the economics faculty and traditional political economy courses. Many of those who would later form the core of HSE passed through these departments. They developed a methodology for teaching economic theory in a transition economy country. This initiative was supported by a one-year grant from the Soros Foundation in 1989.
By order of the Russian government, on November 27, 1992, the Higher School of Economics was officially established. Initially, it offered only master’s degrees.
In 1996, HSE University opened its first regional campus in Nizhny Novgorod. In the following year, HSE University campuses opened in St. Petersburg and Perm.

Since 1996, HSE’s official mascot has been the crow. The first illustration was created by artist Anna Arenstein and over the years many different designs have been introduced. You can find the crow on HSE souvenirs and awards and sometimes even in the streets of Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, Saint Petersburg, or Perm.
